rooms.about: This year we read stories and true books, learn new sounds and spelling patterns, and write our own stories, letters and opinion pieces.

learn: Good readers read every day. They pick books that are just right. A just-right book has only a few words you do not know.
Try the five finger test. Open a page and read it. Hold up one finger for each word you cannot read. Five fingers means the book is too hard for now.
Before you read, look at the cover and the title. Ask: What might this book be about? This guess is called a prediction.
After you read, tell someone what happened. Tell it in order: first, next, then, last.
units.try: Pick a book at home. Look at the cover and make a prediction. Read three pages. Then tell a grown-up what happened, using the words first, next and last.
check: A guess about what will happen
The last page of a book
In the five finger test, five fingers means the book is…

learn: The vowels are a, e, i, o and u. Every word has at least one vowel sound.
A short vowel says its quick sound. Listen: cat, bed, pig, hot, sun.
A long vowel says its own name. Listen: cake, feet, kite, rope, cube.
Magic e at the end of a word is quiet. It makes the vowel before it say its name. Cap becomes cape. Kit becomes kite. Hop becomes hope.
units.try: Add a magic e to each word and read the new word: tap, pin, cub, not, can. You should get tape, pine, cube, note and cane.
check: Which word has a long a sound?
What happens when you add e to hop?

learn: Sometimes two letters work together to make one vowel sound. We call them vowel teams.
The teams ai and ay say long a, as in rain and play. The teams ee and ea often say long e, as in tree and leaf. The teams oa and ow can say long o, as in boat and snow.
Here is a helpful tip. When two vowels go walking, the first one often does the talking. In boat, you hear the o, not the a.
Some teams make new sounds. Oo says the sound in moon. Ou and ow can say the sound in out and cow.
units.try: Go on a word hunt in a book. Find three words with ee or ea, and three with ai or ay. Read them out loud.
check: Which word has the vowel team ai?
What sound does oa make in boat?

learn: Every story has parts. The characters are the people or animals in the story.
The setting is where and when the story happens. It might be a farm, a city, or a long time ago.
The plot is what happens. A plot has a beginning, a middle and an end.
Most stories have a problem. The characters try to solve it. The solution usually comes near the end.
units.try: Think of a story you know well, like a fairy tale. Name the characters, the setting, the problem and the solution. Draw a picture for each one.
check: What is the setting of a story?
Where does the solution usually come in a story?

learn: Many stories teach a lesson. The lesson is also called the moral. A fable is a short story with a moral, often with talking animals.
In one old fable, a slow turtle beats a fast rabbit in a race. The rabbit stops to nap. The lesson is that slow and steady can win.
Characters have feelings. They change when things happen. Look for clue words like smiled, cried or stomped.
Ask yourself: How does the character feel at the start? How do they feel at the end? Why did that change?
units.try: Read or listen to a short story. Tell how the main character felt at the beginning and at the end. Then say the lesson in one sentence.
check: Which word is a clue that a character is angry?

learn: Nonfiction books tell true facts. They teach us about real things, like sharks, planets or people.
True books have special parts. A table of contents lists the chapters. Headings tell what a part is about. Bold words are important words.
A glossary is a small dictionary at the back of the book. Captions are words under a picture that explain it.
The main topic is what the whole book is about. Each paragraph has a main idea too. Ask: What is this part mostly about?
units.try: Find a nonfiction book or article. Point to a heading, a caption and a bold word. Then say the main topic in a few words.
check: At the back of the book
What are the words under a picture called?

learn: A noun is a person, place, thing or animal. Girl, park, ball and dog are nouns.
Most nouns add s to mean more than one: cats, books. Some add es: boxes, dishes. Some change all the way: one child, two children; one foot, two feet; one mouse, two mice.
A verb is an action word. Run, jump and read are verbs. Past tense tells what already happened. Many verbs add ed: jump, jumped. Some change: run, ran; sit, sat.
An adjective describes a noun. It tells what kind or how many. In the sentence The big red dog barked, big and red are adjectives.
units.try: Look around your room. Name three nouns you see. Add an adjective to each one, like soft pillow. Then say a sentence with a verb for each.
check: What is the plural of child?

learn: A sentence is a complete thought. It starts with a capital letter. It ends with a period, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
A telling sentence ends with a period. An asking sentence ends with a question mark. A strong feeling ends with an exclamation mark.
Capital letters also start names, days, months and places: Maya, Monday, July, Texas.
A contraction squeezes two words into one. An apostrophe takes the place of the missing letters. Do not becomes don't. I am becomes I'm. Cannot becomes can't.
units.try: Write three sentences about your day: one telling, one asking and one exciting. Check each one for a capital letter and the right end mark.
check: Which mark ends an asking sentence?
What is the contraction for do not?

learn: A narrative is a story. It can be real or made up. It tells events in order.
Use time words to show order: first, next, then, after that, finally.
Add details so the reader can picture it. Tell what you saw, heard and felt. Instead of It was fun, write I laughed so hard my belly hurt.
End your story in a way that feels finished. You can tell how things turned out or how you felt.
units.try: Write a story about a time you learned something new, like riding a bike. Use at least three time words. Add one detail about how you felt.
check: Which is a time word for a story?
What helps a reader picture your story?

learn: An opinion is what you think or feel. In opinion writing, you tell your opinion and give reasons. Use the word because.
End opinion writing by saying your opinion again. Example: Dogs are the best pets because they love to play. That is why I think dogs are great.
A friendly letter has five parts: the date, the greeting like Dear Sam, the body, the closing like Your friend, and your name.
To write a report, read about a topic first. Write down facts in your own words. Then put the facts into sentences.
units.try: Write a friendly letter to a family member. Tell them your favorite season and give two reasons why. Remember all five parts of a letter.
check: What word helps you give a reason?
Which is the greeting of a letter?

rooms.about: This year we learn place value up to 1,000, add and subtract within 100 and beyond, measure length, tell time, count money, read graphs and explore shapes and equal parts.

learn: Knowing facts like 7 + 6 fast helps with bigger math. By the end of second grade, you can add and subtract within 20 in your head.
Use doubles. If you know 6 + 6 = 12, then 6 + 7 is one more. It is 13.
Make a ten. For 8 + 5, take 2 from the 5 to make 8 into 10. Then 10 + 3 = 13.
Adding and subtracting are a family. If 9 + 4 = 13, then 13 − 4 = 9 and 13 − 9 = 4.
units.try: Solve 9 + 6 by making a ten. Step 1: 9 needs 1 more to make 10. Step 2: Take 1 from the 6, leaving 5. Step 3: 10 + 5 = 15. So 9 + 6 = 15.

learn: An even number can be split into two equal groups. You can also pair up all the objects with none left over.
An odd number always has one left over when you make pairs.
Even numbers end in 0, 2, 4, 6 or 8. Odd numbers end in 1, 3, 5, 7 or 9.
Every even number is a double. 8 = 4 + 4. 10 = 5 + 5.
units.try: Get 11 small things, like buttons. Put them in pairs. Is one left over? Yes, so 11 is odd. Now try 12. All in pairs, so 12 is even. Write 12 as a double: 6 + 6.
check: How can you write 16 as a double?

learn: A three-digit number has hundreds, tens and ones. In 352, the 3 means 3 hundreds, the 5 means 5 tens and the 2 means 2 ones.
Ten ones make one ten. Ten tens make one hundred. Ten hundreds make one thousand.
We can write a number in expanded form. 352 = 300 + 50 + 2.
To compare numbers, look at the hundreds first. Use the signs: > means greater than, < means less than, = means equal. 452 > 425 because they have the same hundreds and 5 tens is more than 2 tens.
units.try: Write 607 in expanded form. Step 1: The 6 is in the hundreds place, so 600. Step 2: There are 0 tens. Step 3: There are 7 ones. So 607 = 600 + 7.

learn: Skip counting means counting by a number other than 1. It is a fast way to count groups.
You can start at any number. Counting by 10s from 23 goes 23, 33, 43, 53. Only the tens digit changes.
Counting by 100s from 140 goes 140, 240, 340. Only the hundreds digit changes.
units.try: Count nickels by 5s. You have 6 nickels. Say 5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30. That is 30 cents.
check: Count by 10s from 47. What comes after 57?

learn: To add two-digit numbers, add the ones, then add the tens.
If the ones add up to 10 or more, make a new ten. This is called regrouping. Carry the new ten to the tens place.
Example: 38 + 25. Ones: 8 + 5 = 13. That is 1 ten and 3 ones. Write 3, carry 1 ten. Tens: 3 + 2 + 1 = 6. The answer is 63.
You can also break numbers apart. 38 + 25 = 30 + 20 + 8 + 5 = 50 + 13 = 63.
units.try: Solve 46 + 37. Step 1: Ones: 6 + 7 = 13. Write 3, carry 1. Step 2: Tens: 4 + 3 + 1 = 8. Step 3: The answer is 83.
check: When the ones add up to 14, what do you do?

learn: To subtract, start with the ones. Then subtract the tens.
If there are not enough ones, break apart a ten. Trade 1 ten for 10 ones. This is also called regrouping.
Example: 52 − 17. You cannot take 7 from 2. Trade a ten: now 4 tens and 12 ones. 12 − 7 = 5. 4 − 1 = 3. The answer is 35.
Check by adding. 35 + 17 = 52, so the answer is right.
units.try: Solve 61 − 28. Step 1: 1 is less than 8, so trade a ten. Now 5 tens and 11 ones. Step 2: 11 − 8 = 3. Step 3: 5 − 2 = 3. The answer is 33. Check: 33 + 28 = 61.

learn: Bigger numbers work the same way. Add or subtract hundreds with hundreds, tens with tens and ones with ones.
Example: 243 + 135. Hundreds: 200 + 100 = 300. Tens: 40 + 30 = 70. Ones: 3 + 5 = 8. The sum is 378.
You can add or take away 10 or 100 in your head. 456 + 10 = 466. 456 + 100 = 556.
Word problems tell a story. Find the numbers. Decide: Are things joining together, or being taken away?
units.try: A school has 325 books. It gets 140 more. How many now? Step 1: 300 + 100 = 400. Step 2: 20 + 40 = 60. Step 3: 5 + 0 = 5. Total: 465 books.

learn: Length tells how long something is. We use a ruler to measure.
Inches and feet are customary units. 12 inches make 1 foot. 3 feet make 1 yard.
Centimeters and meters are metric units. 100 centimeters make 1 meter.
Line up the end of the object with 0 on the ruler. Read the number at the other end. Always write the unit, like 6 inches.
units.try: Measure a spoon with a ruler. Line the end up with 0. Read the number at the tip. Then measure a pencil. Which is longer, and by how many inches?
check: How many inches are in 1 foot?
Which unit is best for measuring a pencil?

learn: A clock has an hour hand and a minute hand. The short hand shows the hour. The long hand shows the minutes.
Count the minutes by 5s. When the long hand points to 3, it is 15 minutes past. Times from midnight to noon are a.m. Times from noon to midnight are p.m.
Coins have values. A penny is 1 cent. A nickel is 5 cents. A dime is 10 cents. A quarter is 25 cents.
To count coins, start with the biggest. Two quarters and one dime is 25, 50, 60. That is 60 cents.
units.try: Count these coins: 1 quarter, 2 dimes and 3 pennies. Step 1: 25. Step 2: 35, 45. Step 3: 46, 47, 48. The total is 48 cents.
check: How many cents is a dime?
The long hand points to 6. How many minutes past the hour?

learn: A bar graph uses bars to show how many. A picture graph uses small pictures. Read the labels to know what each bar means.
Shapes have sides and corners. A triangle has 3 sides. A quadrilateral has 4. A pentagon has 5. A hexagon has 6. A cube is a solid shape with 6 square faces.
We can cut a shape into equal parts. Two equal parts are halves. Three are thirds. Four are fourths, or quarters.
A rectangle can be split into rows and columns of squares. This is an array. 3 rows of 4 is 4 + 4 + 4 = 12.
units.try: Draw a rectangle. Split it into 2 rows and 3 columns of squares. Count them: 3 + 3 = 6 squares. Now draw a circle and split it into 4 equal parts. Each part is one fourth.
check: How many sides does a hexagon have?
A pizza is cut into 3 equal pieces. Each piece is…

rooms.about: This year we explore what things are made of, how heat changes them, what plants need, where animals live, and how land and water shape the Earth.

learn: Everything around us is made of matter. Matter takes up space.
Materials have properties. A property is something you can notice, like color, shape, hardness or texture.
Some materials bend, like rubber. Some are hard, like wood. Some let light through, like glass. Some soak up water, like a sponge.
We choose materials for their properties. A raincoat is waterproof. A window is clear so we can see out.
units.try: Collect five things: a spoon, a sock, a rock, a paper cup and a rubber band. Sort them by one property, like hard or soft. Then sort them a new way, like bendy or not bendy.
check: Why is glass used for windows?

learn: Matter comes in three main forms. A solid keeps its own shape, like a block.
A liquid flows and takes the shape of its container, like milk in a cup.
A gas spreads out to fill any space, like the air in a balloon. You often cannot see it.
Water can be all three. Ice is solid water. Water from the tap is liquid. Steam from a pot is water as a gas.
units.try: Pour some water into a tall glass, then into a bowl. Watch how the water takes the shape of each one. That is what liquids do. Now look at an ice cube in each. Does it change shape?
check: Which one takes the shape of its container?

learn: Heating and cooling can change materials.
Some changes can be undone. Ice melts into water when warm. Freeze the water and it becomes ice again. Chocolate melts and gets hard again when cool.
Some changes cannot be undone. When you cook an egg, it cannot go back to raw. When paper burns, it turns to ash.
Always ask a grown-up before using heat. Stoves, ovens and flames can burn you.
units.try: With a grown-up, put one ice cube on a plate in the sun and one in the shade. Check every 10 minutes. Which melts first? Then put the water in the freezer. Does it turn back to ice?

learn: Big things can be made from many small pieces. A house can be made of many bricks.
You can take the pieces apart and build something new. A pile of blocks can become a tower, then a bridge.
The pieces stay the same. Only the shape of what you built changes.
This is true for matter too. Many tiny pieces fit together to make the things we see.
units.try: Use building blocks or cups to build a tower. Count the pieces. Take it apart and build a bridge with the same pieces. Did the number of pieces change?
check: You take apart a block house and build a car. What stays the same?
What can a house be made from?

learn: Plants are living things. They need water, sunlight, air and space to grow.
Plants use sunlight to make their own food. That is why they grow toward the light.
Roots take in water from the soil. The stem carries water up to the leaves.
Scientists test ideas. Give one plant light and keep one in the dark. Water both the same. The plant in the light grows better.
units.try: Plant two bean seeds in two cups of soil. Put one by a sunny window and one in a dark closet. Water both the same. Check them every day for two weeks and draw what you see.
check: Take in water from the soil
Why do plants grow toward light?
They use sunlight to make food

learn: Many plants make seeds. A seed can grow into a new plant.
Seeds travel to new places. Wind carries dandelion seeds. Some seeds stick to animal fur. Birds eat berries and drop the seeds far away.
Flowers need pollen from other flowers to make seeds. Pollen is a yellow powder.
Bees, butterflies and hummingbirds carry pollen as they drink nectar. This is called pollination.
units.try: Look closely at a fruit like an apple or a tomato with a grown-up. Find the seeds. Count them. How might these seeds travel in nature?
check: What do bees carry from flower to flower?

learn: A habitat is the place where a plant or animal lives. It gives them food, water and shelter.
Different habitats hold different living things. A desert is dry and has cactus and lizards. An ocean has fish and whales. A rainforest is wet and warm, with many kinds of plants and animals.
Living things are suited to their habitat. A polar bear has thick fur for the cold. A camel can go days without drinking.
Many kinds of life in one place is called biodiversity. Rainforests have more kinds of living things than almost anywhere.
units.try: Go outside and look at a small patch of ground, like a yard or park. Count how many kinds of plants and animals you find. Draw them and name your habitat.
check: What does a habitat give an animal?
Which animal is suited to the cold?

learn: Earth has many landforms. A mountain is very high land. A valley is low land between hills. A plain is wide and flat.
Most of Earth is covered by water. Oceans hold salt water. Lakes, rivers and ponds usually hold fresh water.
Water on Earth can be solid or liquid. Glaciers and ice caps are frozen water.
A map shows land and water from above. Blue usually shows water. A key explains the symbols.
units.try: Make a model landscape in a tray with sand or dirt. Build a mountain, a valley and a flat plain. Pour a little water at the top of the mountain. Where does it go?
check: What color usually shows water on a map?

learn: The Earth is always changing. Some changes are fast. Some are very slow.
Fast changes happen in hours or days. Earthquakes shake the ground. Volcanoes erupt. Floods can wash away land.
Slow changes take many years. Wind and water wear rocks away bit by bit. This is called erosion. A river took millions of years to carve the Grand Canyon.
People can slow erosion. Plants hold soil with their roots. Walls and fences can block wind and water.
units.try: Make two small hills of dirt in pans. Press grass or leaves into one. Gently sprinkle water on both. Which hill loses more dirt? That shows how plants slow erosion.

learn: An engineer solves problems by designing things. You can think like an engineer too.
First, ask: What is the problem? Next, imagine ideas. Then plan and draw one idea.
Build it and test it. Did it work? If not, change it and try again. This is called improving a design.
Comparing two designs helps. Test them the same way and see which works better.
units.try: Design a paper bridge between two books. Test how many coins it holds. Then fold the paper into a zigzag and test again. Which design held more?
check: What is the first step an engineer takes?
Your design did not work. What should you do?

rooms.about: This year we learn about communities, maps, how goods are made and traded, government and rules, and people from the past who made a difference.

learn: A community is a place where people live, work and play together.

There are three kinds of communities. A city, or urban community, has many people and tall buildings. A suburb is near a city and has many houses. A rural community is in the country, with farms and open land.
People in a community help each other. They share parks, schools, roads and libraries.
Every community is a little different. Some are by the sea. Some are in the mountains.
units.try: Draw a picture of your community. Show your home and three places your family goes, like a store, a park or a library. Is your community urban, suburban or rural?
check: A community near a city with many houses

learn: A map is a drawing of a place from above. A globe is a round model of the Earth.
A compass rose shows directions: north, south, east and west. North is usually at the top of a map.
A map key, or legend, explains the symbols. A tiny tree might mean a park.
Earth has seven continents and five oceans. We live in North America. The Pacific is the largest ocean.
units.try: Draw a map of your bedroom from above. Add a compass rose. Make a key with symbols for your bed, door and window.
check: What does a map key tell you?
Which continent is the United States in?

learn: The United States has 50 states. Each state has a capital city.
The capital of our whole country is Washington, D.C. The President lives and works there in the White House.
Our country has many landforms: the Rocky Mountains, the Great Plains, the Mississippi River and long coastlines.
Weather and land affect how people live. People near the sea may fish. People on plains may farm.
units.try: Find your state on a map of the United States. Name its capital city. Then find one river or mountain range in your state.
check: How many states are in the United States?
What is the capital of the United States?

learn: Needs are things we must have to live: food, water, clothes and shelter.
Wants are things we would like but can live without, like toys or games.
People cannot have everything they want. Choosing one thing means giving up another. This is called a choice.
Saving means keeping money to use later. Families often save for big things.
units.try: Make two lists: needs and wants. Put at least four things on each list. Then pretend you have 5 dollars. Which one want would you choose, and what would you give up?

learn: Goods are things people make or grow, like bread, shoes and apples.
Services are jobs people do for others, like teaching, fixing cars or cutting hair.
Producers make goods or give services. Consumers buy and use them. You are a consumer when you buy a snack.
People trade to get what they need. Long ago, people often traded goods directly. This is called barter. Today we usually use money.
units.try: Think of three workers in your community. For each one, say if they make goods or give a service. For example, a baker makes goods and a doctor gives a service.
check: Someone who buys and uses goods

learn: Most food travels a long way to get to you.
Take milk. A farmer milks the cows. A truck takes the milk to a factory. The factory cleans it and puts it in cartons. Trucks bring it to stores. Then your family buys it.
Many people help along the way: farmers, drivers, factory workers and store clerks.
Some foods come from other countries. Bananas often come from Central and South America, where it is warm all year.
units.try: Pick a food in your kitchen. Draw the steps it took to reach you, from where it grew to your table. Show at least four steps.
check: Why do bananas often come from warm places?
They grow where it is warm all year

learn: Rules keep us safe and fair. Families and schools have rules.
Laws are rules for a whole community or country. Police officers help people follow laws.
A government makes laws and runs services. A city often has a mayor. A state has a governor. The country has a President.
Citizens are members of a country. In the United States, adult citizens vote to choose many leaders.
units.try: Make up three fair rules for a game or for your home. Explain why each rule is helpful. Ask your family to vote on which rule is most important.
check: What do citizens do to choose leaders?

learn: A good citizen helps the community. They follow rules and treat others with respect.
Good citizens are honest. They tell the truth and take care of shared places.
You can help by picking up litter, recycling and being kind to neighbors.
Our country has symbols. The flag has 50 stars, one for each state, and 13 stripes for the first 13 colonies. The bald eagle is our national bird.
units.try: Do one helpful thing for your community this week, like picking up litter with a grown-up or making a card for a neighbor. Tell someone how it helped.
check: What do the 50 stars on the flag stand for?
Which is a way to be a good citizen?

learn: History is the story of the past. Life long ago was very different.
Long ago, people used candles and oil lamps for light. Today we use electric lights. People wrote letters by hand. Today many people send messages on phones.
Some things have stayed the same. Families still eat together, play games and go to school.
We learn about the past from old photos, letters, tools and stories from older people.
units.try: Interview a grandparent or an older adult. Ask: What games did you play as a child? How did you get to school? Write down two things that changed and one that stayed the same.
check: What did people use for light long ago?
How can we learn about the past?

learn: Many people have worked to make life better for others.
Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat on a bus in 1955. At that time, unfair laws kept Black people separate from white people. Her courage helped change those laws.
Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led peaceful marches and gave speeches for equal rights. Cesar Chavez worked so farm workers would be treated fairly.
Inventors made a difference too. George Washington Carver found hundreds of uses for peanuts and helped farmers grow healthier soil.
units.try: Choose one person from this unit. Draw a picture of them and write one sentence about how they made life better for others.
check: What did Rosa Parks do in 1955?
Refused to give up her bus seat
Who worked so farm workers were treated fairly?

rooms.about: This year we explore line, shape, color, texture and pattern, try drawing, painting, printing and building, and look at art from many places.

learn: A line is a mark that moves from one point to another. Lines are the start of most drawings.
Lines can be straight, curved, zigzag, wavy, dotted, thick or thin.
Lines can show feelings. Wavy lines can feel calm. Zigzag lines can feel full of energy.
Artists use lines to show edges, patterns and movement.
units.try: Fold a paper into six boxes. Fill each box with a different kind of line: straight, curved, zigzag, wavy, dotted and spiral. Which one feels the most calm?
check: Which line might feel full of energy?
A mark from one point to another

learn: A shape is flat. It has length and width. Circles, squares and triangles are geometric shapes.
Organic shapes are free and curvy, like leaves, clouds and puddles.
A form is not flat. It has height, width and depth. A ball is a sphere. A box is a cube.
Artists build pictures from simple shapes. A cat can start as a circle head and an oval body.
units.try: Draw an animal using only shapes. Start with a big oval for the body and a circle for the head. Add triangles for ears and rectangles for legs.
check: What does a form have that a shape does not?

learn: The primary colors are red, yellow and blue. You cannot mix other paints to make them.
Mix two primary colors to make a secondary color. Red and yellow make orange. Yellow and blue make green. Blue and red make violet.
A color wheel shows colors in a circle. Colors next to each other look calm together.
Add white to make a tint, a lighter color. Add black to make a shade, a darker color.
units.try: With paint or crayons, make a small color wheel. Put red, yellow and blue in a circle. Mix the colors between them to make orange, green and violet.
check: What do yellow and blue make?

learn: Warm colors are red, orange and yellow. They remind us of fire and sunshine.
Cool colors are blue, green and violet. They remind us of water, grass and ice.
Warm colors can feel exciting. Cool colors can feel calm or quiet.
Artists choose colors to set a mood, or feeling, in their art.
units.try: Draw the same tree twice. Color one with only warm colors and one with only cool colors. How does each tree make you feel?
check: What do artists use colors to set?

learn: Texture is how something feels, or looks like it would feel. It can be rough, smooth, bumpy, soft or fuzzy.
Real texture is what you feel when you touch it, like tree bark.
Implied texture is drawn. Short lines can look like fur. Little dots can look like sand.
A rubbing copies texture. Lay paper over a bumpy surface and rub a crayon on its side.
units.try: Make texture rubbings. Put thin paper over a leaf, a coin, or a rough wall. Rub with the side of a crayon. Collect five textures and label each one.

learn: A pattern is something that repeats. It can be a line, shape or color.
A simple pattern could be red, blue, red, blue. This is called an AB pattern. An ABC pattern has three parts.
Patterns are found in nature, like stripes on a zebra or spots on a ladybug.
People around the world use patterns in cloth, pottery and buildings.
units.try: Make a paper bookmark. Decorate it with a repeating pattern of shapes and colors, like circle, star, circle, star. Can someone guess what comes next?
check: Where can you find a pattern in nature?

learn: Artists look closely before they draw. This is called observation.
Look at the big shapes first. Then add the smaller details.
Objects in front can overlap, or cover part of, objects behind them. Overlapping shows which is closer.
Things far away look smaller. Things close look bigger.
units.try: Set up three fruits on a table, with one in front of the others. Look closely for one minute. Draw the big shapes, then add details. Show which fruit is in front by overlapping.
check: How do you show one thing is in front?

learn: A print is made by pressing a painted surface onto paper. You can make many copies.
You can print with almost anything: sponges, leaves, corks or carved foam.
Put a thin layer of paint on the object. Press it down firmly. Lift it straight up.
Printmakers often repeat prints to make patterns.
units.try: With a grown-up, cut a potato in half. Have the grown-up carve a simple shape into it. Dip it in paint and press it on paper. Make a pattern with your prints.
check: What is special about a print?
How should you lift a print?

learn: A sculpture is 3D art. You can walk around it and see all sides.
Sculptures can be made from clay, wood, stone, metal or paper.
Adding material is called building up. Removing material, like carving, is called taking away.
Clay can be pinched, rolled into coils or flattened into slabs.
units.try: Make a small pinch pot. Roll clay or play dough into a ball. Push your thumb in the middle. Pinch around and around to make the walls thin and even.
check: 3D art you can see from all sides
Which is a way to shape clay?

learn: People everywhere make art. Art tells stories about how people live and what they value.
In Mexico, artists make bright papel picado, which is paper cut into lacy designs for celebrations.
In Japan, people fold paper into shapes. This is called origami. A paper crane is a famous origami shape.
Many Native American nations make beautiful beadwork, baskets and pottery with meaningful designs.
units.try: Fold a square of paper in half, then in half again. Cut small shapes along the folds with safe scissors. Open it up to see a lacy design like papel picado.

rooms.about: This year we feel the beat, read simple rhythms, sing high and low, learn about instruments and enjoy music from many places.

learn: The beat is the steady pulse of music. It is like a heartbeat. It keeps going, even, again and again.
You can feel the beat by clapping, tapping or marching.
Some music has a fast beat. Some has a slow beat. How fast the beat goes is called tempo.
Allegro means fast. Largo means very slow.
units.try: Play a song you like. Pat your knees to the steady beat. Now march around the room to the beat. Is the tempo fast or slow?

learn: Rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds. The words of a song have a rhythm.
A quarter note is one sound on one beat. We can say ta.
Two eighth notes share one beat. They are quick. We can say ti-ti.
A quarter rest is one beat of silence. Rests are important. They give the music a breath.
units.try: Clap this rhythm: ta, ta, ti-ti, ta. Then clap: ta, ti-ti, ta, rest. Make sure your rest is silent but still takes one beat.
check: How many eighth notes fit in one beat?

learn: Pitch is how high or low a sound is. A bird chirp is high. A big drum is low.
Melody is a line of pitches, one after another. It is the tune you hum.
A melody can go up, go down or stay the same.
Musicians use names for pitches. Many children learn so, mi and la first.
units.try: Sing a song you know. Move your hand up when the tune goes higher and down when it goes lower. Then sing so-mi-so-mi like calling someone's name.
check: How high or low a sound is

learn: Dynamics tell how loud or soft music is.
Forte means loud. It is written f. Piano means soft. It is written p.
Crescendo means slowly get louder. Decrescendo means slowly get softer.
Music changes dynamics to show feelings. A lullaby is soft. A parade march is loud.
units.try: Say a nursery rhyme very softly, piano. Say it again loudly, forte. Then start soft and grow louder each line, a crescendo.

learn: You have four voices: whisper, speaking, calling and singing.
To sing well, stand tall and relax your shoulders. Take a deep breath into your belly.
Open your mouth and let the sound float out. Do not shout. Shouting can hurt your voice.
Drink water to keep your voice healthy.
units.try: Stand tall and take a slow breath. Sing a simple song, like a birthday song. Try using your whisper voice, then your speaking voice, then your singing voice.
check: What should you do before you sing?
Why should you not shout when you sing?

learn: Instruments are grouped in families. In the string family, strings shake to make sound, like the violin and cello.
In the woodwind family, players blow air, like the flute and clarinet.
In the brass family, players buzz their lips into a metal mouthpiece, like the trumpet and tuba.
In the percussion family, players hit, shake or scrape, like drums and tambourines.
units.try: Make a shaker. Put dry rice in a plastic bottle and tighten the lid. Which family is it in? Play it to the beat of a song.
check: Which family is the trumpet in?

learn: Music is made of parts. Some parts repeat. Some parts are new. This is called form.
We use letters to name parts. If a part repeats, it gets the same letter.
AB form has two different parts. ABA form has a part, a new part, then the first part again.
Many songs have a verse and a chorus. The chorus usually repeats with the same words.
units.try: Make up an ABA dance. For A, clap four times. For B, stomp four times. Then do A again. Can you add a C part?
check: In ABA form, what comes last?
What part of a song usually repeats with the same words?

learn: Music can tell a story without words. This is called program music.
In one famous piece for children, each animal is played by a different instrument. A bird might be a flute. A grandfather might be a bassoon.
Composers use fast or slow tempo, loud or soft sounds and high or low notes to show a character.
Movies use music too. It tells you when to feel scared, happy or excited.
units.try: Pick an animal. Choose a sound for it: high or low, fast or slow, loud or soft. Make the sound with your voice or a homemade instrument and see if someone can guess the animal.
check: What might a high fast sound show?

learn: People everywhere make music. Each place has its own sounds and instruments.
In West Africa, drummers play rhythms together, often with call and response. One person sings or plays, and the group answers.
Mariachi music from Mexico uses trumpets, violins and guitars.
In the United States, jazz began in New Orleans. It was created mainly by Black musicians and mixes many styles.
units.try: Play call and response with a family member. You clap a short rhythm. They copy it. Then switch. Keep going and make the rhythms a little harder.
check: One person leads and the group answers
In which city did jazz begin?

learn: Composers write their own music. You can be a composer too.
Start with a steady beat. Then add a rhythm using ta, ti-ti and rests.
Add a melody with high and low sounds. Repeat parts you like.
You can write your music down with pictures or symbols so you can play it again.
units.try: Make a four-beat rhythm using ta, ti-ti and rest. Write it down with your own symbols. Play it on a pot with a wooden spoon, then teach it to someone.
check: So you can play it again

rooms.about: This year we move our bodies in new ways, learn to throw, catch and balance, and learn how to stay clean, safe, healthy and kind.

learn: Before you play, look for your space. Your personal space is the bubble around you. Keep your arms out of other people's bubbles.
Warm up first. A warm-up gets your heart and muscles ready. Jog in place or do arm circles.
Wear the right shoes and tie your laces. Drink water when you play.
Stop if something hurts. Tell a grown-up.
units.try: Make your personal space bubble by spinning slowly with arms out. Then warm up: 20 seconds of jogging in place, 10 arm circles forward and 10 backward.
check: To get our heart and muscles ready
What should you do if something hurts?

learn: Locomotor skills move you from place to place. Walking, running, hopping, jumping, skipping, galloping and sliding are locomotor skills.
A hop is on one foot. A jump uses two feet.
To skip, step and hop on one foot, then step and hop on the other.
You can change speed, from slow to fast. You can change level, from low to high.
units.try: In a safe space, try each move for 10 steps: hop on your right foot, hop on your left foot, jump, gallop and skip. Which was hardest?
check: How many feet do you use to hop?

learn: Balance means staying steady without falling.
It is easier to balance on a wide base, like two feet apart. It is harder on a small base, like one foot.
Hold your arms out and look at one spot to help you balance.
Strong belly muscles help with balance.
units.try: Stand on one foot and count to 10. Switch feet. Now try with your eyes looking at one spot on the wall. Can you count to 20?
check: Which is easiest to balance on?

learn: To throw overhand, stand sideways to your target. Hold the ball by your ear.
Step forward with the foot opposite your throwing arm. Then throw and point your hand at the target.
To catch, watch the ball. Hold your hands out with fingers spread.
For a high ball, thumbs touch. For a low ball, pinkies touch. Pull the ball in to your body.
units.try: Use a soft ball or rolled-up socks. Toss it to a partner from 5 big steps away. Each time you both catch it, take one step back.
check: Which foot steps forward when you throw with your right arm?
What should you watch when catching?

learn: Jumping rope makes your heart strong.
Hold the handles at your hips. Turn the rope with your wrists, not your whole arms.
Jump just high enough to let the rope pass. Land softly on the balls of your feet.
Count your jumps. Try to beat your own record.
units.try: If you have a jump rope, jump 10 times in a row. If not, pretend to turn a rope and jump softly on the balls of your feet 20 times.
check: How should you land when jumping rope?
Softly on the balls of your feet

learn: Your heart is a muscle. It pumps blood all through your body.
When you run and play, your heart beats faster. You breathe harder too.
Kids should be active for at least 60 minutes every day.
You can feel your heartbeat. Put two fingers on the side of your neck.
units.try: Feel your heartbeat while sitting. Then do 30 jumping jacks. Feel it again. Is it faster? Rest for one minute and feel it slow down.
check: How many minutes should kids be active each day?
What happens to your heart when you run?

learn: Germs are tiny living things that can make us sick. They are too small to see.
Wash your hands with soap and water for 20 seconds. That is about as long as singing the birthday song twice.
Wash before eating and after using the bathroom.
Cover coughs and sneezes with your elbow. Brush your teeth two times a day for two minutes.
units.try: Wash your hands the right way. Wet them, add soap, scrub the backs, between fingers and under nails while singing the birthday song twice. Rinse and dry.
check: How long should you wash your hands?

learn: Food gives you energy to grow, learn and play.
There are five food groups: fruits, vegetables, grains, protein foods and dairy.
Try to fill half your plate with fruits and vegetables.
Water is the best drink. Sweets and soda are treats for sometimes, not every day.
units.try: Look at your lunch or dinner. Name the food groups on your plate. Which group is missing? Plan one way to add it tomorrow.
check: How much of your plate should be fruits and vegetables?

learn: Wear a helmet when you ride a bike or scooter.
Buckle your seat belt in the car. Kids should ride in the back seat.
Cross streets with a grown-up. Stop, look left, look right and look left again.
Know your address and a grown-up's phone number. In an emergency, call 911.
units.try: Practice saying your full address and a grown-up's phone number. Then practice stop, look left, look right, look left again with a grown-up on a safe sidewalk.
check: What number do you call in an emergency?
What should you wear when riding a bike?

learn: Everyone has feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared and excited. All feelings are okay.
What we do with feelings matters. When you are angry, stop and take three slow breaths.
Use words to say how you feel. Say: I feel sad when you leave me out.
Be a good friend. Take turns, share, listen and include others. If someone is being bullied, tell a trusted adult.
units.try: Practice belly breathing. Put a hand on your belly. Breathe in slowly for 4 counts and feel it rise. Breathe out for 4 counts. Do it 3 times.
check: What can you do when you feel angry?
What should you do if someone is being bullied?
